title: Agents That Answer the Phone and Sign the Forms
description: Nine new tools where the agent stops writing code and acts on the outside world: inboxes, phone lines, shops, payments, boards, CAD and a blog.
tldr: Pidgeon gives agents their own email inboxes with a firewall on inbound mail, Crulon answers a business phone line and hands calls to your team, StoreRouter lets a CLI or MCP client search and parse real shops, and Nevermined charges per agent call in fiat or crypto. Cirkit reads schematic PDFs against your BOM, Amni-CAD runs parametric CAD with FEA and CFD in a browser tab that Claude can drive, SlopIt hands your agent a blog to publish to, UserRank shows the skills other builders actually run, and SkillScout recommends tools against your gaps instead of a popularity list.
content:
# Agents That Answer the Phone and Sign the Forms

Most of the agent tooling that arrives on Hacker News is still about code: how the agent edits a file, how it keeps context, how it survives a long run. The batch below is different. Each of these nine tools hands the agent something outside the codebase, an inbox, a phone line, a shop catalog, a payment rail, a schematic, a CAD model, a blog, and then has to answer the question that follows: who is accountable when the agent acts there.

## An inbox of its own

[[link:/tools/2186|Pidgeon]] starts from the observation that an agent with an email address can do a surprising amount of ordinary business. Send mail at volume from an address that belongs to the agent, read what arrives, answer inside the same thread, keep a calendar by mail, pull the details out of invoices and attachments, and hand the thread to a person when it needs one. The interesting design decision is the Firewall: every inbound message is screened before it reaches the agent, and every confirmation code that arrives from a third-party signup comes with a verdict attached. That matters because one of the more useful things an agent can do with its own address is register for other tools, and you would rather it did that with its own credentials than yours. Mail is hosted in the EU and is not trained on.

## The line is answered by an agent

[[link:/tools/2201|Crulon]] puts the agent on a business phone line instead of behind a chat box. A call enters a Call Flow and, out of hours, goes to the agent, which answers, does the work in the tools you have given it, and hands the call to a human with a summary. The part that separates it from an answering service is live visibility: your team sees every call as it happens and can take over any one of them. You supply the voice, a greeting, your files or website, and the Tools the agent is allowed to use. It starts at $24 a seat.

## Shopping through a terminal

[[link:/tools/2197|StoreRouter]] is what an agent needs before it can buy anything: product search across covered domains, a Parse endpoint that returns a token-efficient version of any product page, lookup by URL, and similar products across domains. There is a CLI, a REST API, Python and TypeScript SDKs, and an MCP connection, and a browser playground runs the real CLI so you can try it before installing. The Parse endpoint is the telling one. A raw product page is mostly chrome, and handing one to a model wastes the context window on navigation and tracking markup.

## Getting paid per call

[[link:/tools/2210|Nevermined]] is the money layer underneath all of this. You register agents, design usage-based plans, and accept payment in fiat or crypto from any consumer over HTTP-native x402, with MCP and A2A access alongside it. Per-seat pricing does not survive contact with software that runs unattended, so a platform that charges per call is the shape this has to take eventually.

## A schematic, read against your BOM

[[link:/tools/2207|Cirkit]] takes the PDF your EDA tool already exports and turns it into a shared workspace: BOM-aware parts, notes the whole team can search, equations that use real part values, trace maps across boards, and proposed changes sketched onto the drawing. The AI reads the page and answers against your BOM rather than the internet's guess, which is the only way an answer about a resistor divider is worth anything. There is nothing to install, and multi-page and multi-board projects are welcome.

## CAD in a browser tab, driven by Claude

[[link:/tools/2202|Amni-CAD]] is free parametric 3D CAD that runs in the browser, built on OpenCascade solids with STEP export, GPU stress and modal analysis, a wind-tunnel CFD pass, and automatic 2D drawings with tolerances. The AI assistant connects to Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or a local model, so an external agent can drive the geometry over MCP. Having the solver in the same tab as the model removes the export-import ritual that usually sits between designing a part and checking it.

## The blog writes itself

[[link:/tools/2199|SlopIt]] is the smallest idea here and one of the clearest. Your agent signs up, writes a post, and sends back a live link. Free on a slopit.io subdomain, your own domain on Pro, and the core is MIT licensed and self-hostable as REST plus MCP over static HTML and one SQLite file. There is no editor to log into, which is the point: the posts are written by the thing that already knows what you shipped, and they land as crawlable pages rather than a changelog nobody reads.

## What everyone else is running

[[link:/tools/2192|UserRank]] answers a question most people answer badly: what do other people actually have installed? Your own Claude or ChatGPT scans locally and only names and counts leave your machine, then the site shows the tools, skills and MCP servers other builders run. It is in beta and the full scan takes ten to twenty minutes, but the privacy model, scan locally, publish counts, is the one you want for this kind of comparison.

## Choosing tools against your own gaps

[[link:/tools/2211|SkillScout]] takes the same problem from the other end. It asks the AI you already use how you work, scores every tool in its index against the gaps it finds, and hands back a short list. Free, and deliberately not a popularity ranking. The failure mode of every best-of list is that it recommends the same ten tools to everyone, and a recommendation that ignores what you already do is not a recommendation.

## What they all have in common

Look at what each of these had to build beyond the model call. Pidgeon built a Firewall. Crulon built live takeover. StoreRouter built a parser. Nevermined built a payment rail. Cirkit built BOM awareness. Amni-CAD built a solver. SlopIt built a publishing target. The agent is the easy part; the accountability layer around it is the product. That is the pattern worth watching: as agents move from suggesting to acting, the interesting engineering moves to the handoff, the receipt, and the moment a person takes back control.
